extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys/agents and patent drafters practicing in the U.S. (claim drafting/prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting patent claims to maximize claim scope while avoiding U.S.-specific pitfalls (112(f), written description, limiting language). Focuses on claim language choices and supporting specification strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strip Out Adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Most adjectives in claims are limiting and unnecessary. "A user-friendly graphical interface" - delete "user-friendly." "A high-performance processor" - delete "high-performance." Each adjective is something an accused product can lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid non-functional, descriptive adjectives that narrow claim scope. When an adjective is not required to distinguish prior art or define the invention's operation, remove it. Examples: remove "user-friendly," "high-performance." Anti-pattern: relying on marketing adjectives to define elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Claiming Carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting elements by what they do (rather than what they are) is broader - but invokes 112(f) risk in U.S. practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To gain breadth while minimizing 112(f) (means-plus-function) risk, pair functional language with one or more concrete structural recitations (example: "a sensor configured to detect X, the sensor comprising Y"). Balance functional phrasing with structural detail and ensure the spec supports the functions/structures recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus, Not Species
rubrics_metrics.description: If your invention works with springs, do not claim "a coil spring." Claim "a biasing element" - and disclose, as alternatives, coil springs, leaf springs, elastomer pads, gas springs. Each species disclosure supports a genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim broader categories (genus) rather than specific species when appropriate, and in the specification disclose multiple representative species as alternatives to support the genus. Practical tip: disclose examples of different species to provide written-description support for the genus claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Numerical Limits Unless Necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: "At least 50% by weight" is a hard limit; an accused product at 49.9% does not infringe. If the number is not load-bearing for novelty, leave it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude precise numeric limits unless required to distinguish prior art or define a necessary functional boundary. If numerical limits are needed, disclose ranges and multiple endpoints in the spec to allow claim flexibility. Be mindful that single-point numbers create hard, often unnecessary boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch Out for "Configured To" vs. "For"
rubrics_metrics.description: "A processor for performing X" may invoke 112(f) post-Williamson; "a processor configured to perform X" plus a clear algorithmic disclosure in the spec is safer. The choice has scope consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose phrasing carefully: "for" can be interpreted as functional language that triggers 112(f) under current case law; "configured to" is often preferable but requires accompanying disclosure (e.g., algorithmic steps) to support the claimed functionality. Consider how courts have interpreted the phrasing in your jurisdiction and ensure the spec provides concrete support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Describing the Environment as a Limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a widget that says "for use in an automobile" - is the automobile a limitation? Maybe. If you do not need the automobile to distinguish prior art, do not include it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include environmental or intended-use language that could be read as a claim limitation unless necessary. Only recite environment or field-of-use when it is essential to novelty or operability; otherwise omit to preserve broader scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Open Transitional Language
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comprising" admits additional unrecited elements. "Including" is treated similarly. "Consisting of" closes the claim. Default to comprising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open transitional phrases (e.g., "comprising," "including") to allow additional, unrecited elements and maximize infringement scope. Use closed transitions (e.g., "consisting of") only when you intentionally want to exclude additional elements. Be explicit about transition terms because they determine openness/closedness of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Be Afraid of a Long Spec to Support Short Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure costs little; claim breadth is determined at the time of drafting and frozen. A 60-page spec supporting a 4-line claim is a fine outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in a detailed specification to support broad, concise claims. Extensive disclosure (examples, embodiments, species) can be used to justify broad claim language and to fend off written-description and enablement challenges later. Practical trade-off: longer spec is inexpensive compared to losing claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware Negative Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wherein the device does not include X" must be supported in the spec by an explicit statement that X is absent. Santarus v. Par (Fed. Cir. 2012). Without spec support, the negative limitation is a 112(b) problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you draft claims that exclude features (negative limitations), ensure the specification expressly supports the absence of the excluded feature. Cite/consider controlling case law (e.g., Santarus v. Par) showing that unsupported negative limitations can be indefiniteness or 112(b) problems. Anti-pattern: adding negatives in claims without corresponding spec language.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Genus-Species Trade-Off in Biotech
rubrics_metrics.description: In biotech, broad genus claims face heightened written-description scrutiny (Amgen v. Sanofi, 2023, on enablement). The lesson generalizes: in unpredictable arts, breadth must be earned by extensive disclosure of representative species and a unifying structural feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable technical fields (especially biotech), claim breadth requires substantial representative disclosure and identification of a unifying structural/functional feature to satisfy written description and enablement. Support genus claims with many species examples and clear explanation of why the genus is enabled. Be mindful of recent case law (e.g., Amgen v. Sanofi) when asserting broad claims in such arts.
